game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wanted to give this a positive review, as someone who loves games like this ( Papers Please! being a personal favorite)

However, I'm very indifferent due to the lack of content and the seemingly linear focus of the story and the severe lack of challenge ( all your options are highlighted for you)

It had a TON of potential and did give a very 1984ish vibe, and I enjoyed the small amounts of content it offered ( 30 minutes an episode?). However if you, like me, go into this expecting a Papers Please! experience you will be severely disappointed.

5/10 ( don't buy unless it is on sale is my reccomendation -- or until all episodes have been unlocked for one continuous playthrough)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Interesting, compelling, and flawed. Contrary to some negative reviews I don't mind the format of Orwell being a linear visual novel, sometimes the best way to tell a complicated story is to tell it simply, and for what it's worth, it works well as long as Orwell is telling the story it thinks it is. 

With that being said, Orwell pulls its biggest punch on its lynchpin issue concerning its closing question on a terrorist attack you've been investigating from the beginning of the story, where, when circling back at the climax, Orwell thinks it's asking you a sensible question. Would I condemn the use of Orwellian nation state surveillance in the face of what we've learned during the story? 

Of course it's something I condemn, we've all a right to privacy.

But in order to answer the question as Orwell wants to phrase it, i found myself being really frustrated with how the game allows you to give your answer, and i'm really disappointed with what feels like really negligent storytelling. 

Orwell isnt as mature as it thinks it is. At the crux of it, Orwell isn't asking you to measure freedom against safety, It asks would you rather be a bootlicker to solve a terror attack killing several and wounding others, or let the perpetrators off because the developers skipped watching minority report?

We've a right to live free from terror, and the real fault of Orwell is that it ends up presenting terror and surveillance as equivalent issues rather than being in tension with one another. You're not asked what would you be willing to do to prevent an act of terror, it's already happened, people have died.

That Orwell also asks if you would like to give the system a middle finger by way of a Watergate sidestep to, again, apprehending conspirators / co-conspirators to a terror attack seems to be completely missing the point.

Am I missing things and details here? Almost certainly, there are a few different endings and granular differences depending on your choices throughout the story that paint a different picture. But for me, Orwell treats 1984 as the only book on the shelf.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The problem I have with this game is that it tries to hold you accountable for choices you did not make. Your task in Orwell is simply to retrieve information, someone will make a decision based on the information you collect. However, you are not in control of when this person makes a decision, so at times your attempt to gather all information to get the full picture are halted midway.  In addition, you are forced to choose between information chunks at crucial moments in the game even though there is no reason why you should. By doing so, the game forces you to not consider the entire context. And what does the game do to you at end? Blame you for not considering the entire context.

Another problem I have with this game is the more philosophical debate of an Orwellian surveillance system. By pretending that there is no separation of power or strict legislation on how evidence may be gathered, the creators abuse the fictive setting to criticize such a system. Yes, such a system would be horrible in certain dictatorship countries that currently exist, but we already know that don't we? It's an interesting concept that can be used for good as well. This nuance is missing in the story and as a result the writers and this game discredit themselves as a worthy piece of fiction.

review_text_raw:
While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

review_text_raw:
The short review: I enjoyed playing this game, but I wouldn't recommend it. You should give it a try and form your own opinion though!

The long review: The game frustrated me because I expected a lot more narrative-wise since they used the name "Orwell". It definitely had parts where it excelled. The art is fantastic. The evidence gathering mechanic is a fun take on the traditional point and click genre. The story maintains a sense of mystery and suspense that can hook you in for the most part. Trying to figure out who Goldfels is and whether or not their intentions are truly malicious was what drove me to keep playing. I loved that there were also little easter eggs, such as a reference to "giraffes in hats" and articles about a 50 shades ripoff movie that made the game world feel more alive.

However, the writing... that's where this game falls short. There are other reviews talking about how the dialogue could be better etc., and I agree with them, but it wasn't the worst thing ever and it didn't ruin my experience. What DID ruin things for me was the game's last chapter. The narrative took a nosedive and the payoff completely ruined the setup. Most other reviews had no issue with the ending though, so you should definitely reserve your judgement and play the game first!


*****Some spoilers ahead*****

Just for context, I've only played this game once, and in my playthrough I prevented the 3rd bomb from exploding and decided to turn in evidence against Catherine Delacroix at the end.

The thing I hated MOST about this last chapter was the twist. Basically, one of the characters go "I was the person behind all those bombings bwahahaha". A real Reiner Braun moment.

This twist ending had two effects. First, it completely undermined the established mystery. Immediately, I felt stupid for caring about the game at all. What was the point of me working so hard then? Why did I collect all that evidence, if the criminal was just going to out themselves like that? 

The second effect was it made the whole narrative thematically unsatisfying. In the ending I received (I don't know if there are other possibilities), the criminal become the leader of the activist group with no repercussions. This was a person who'd set up two bombs that killed people. What pissed me off the most was that this person's friends acknowledges that this person committed murder, but based on the ending, it suggests all of them had decided to look the other way. Apparently, murder and thought manipulation is not a big deal when THEY are the ones doing it. So am I supposed to sympathise with this irresponsible group of people who have showed no regard for human life?? It's feels extremely hypocritical.

It really frustrated me because this game keeps telling me these people are innocent and I'm ruining their lives, but these people clearly aren't innocent. The worst things they did included: killing a police officer, doxxing a government agent, bombing and killing people at two separate locations, then attempting to cover up their crimes. Granted, some of these characters are more justified in their actions, but that doesn't change the fact that they actively ruined or tried to ruin people's lives. The only person I can say is mostly harmless in all of this is Themba. The game could've easily made this more nuanced by adding just one completely innocent character for the player to falsely incriminate. This one change would've easily revealed the flaws of the Orwell surveillance system, but that's not what happened. Instead, the game tries to guilt-trip you into feeling bad for outing people who have ACTUALLY done terrible things.

Maybe I only had a bad experience because my choices sucked. Maybe there is an ending where I get a better experience and justice is served to all, but then that implies there is a "right" way to choose, therefore you SHOULDN'T have the freedom to choose, your thoughts should be RESTRICTED so you choose only what the game thinks is right.

So what exactly is this game trying to tell me?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wish I liked it because on the paper it's 100% a game for me but I'm forced to admit I just don't.

First of all it's not detective work, you just drop pieces of information in a database hoping it makes the story progress.

Because you're not technically forced to drop all the information in the database, you quickly try to have an impact on the story's progression by keeping some info to yourself, but the story only progresses when specific info is used and you never know which info is necessary or not so you can't really make informed choices on what to give Orwell and what to not.

I quickly find myself stuck with the story not progressing because I've decided to keep a piece of information that's mandatory for the story to continue and so I have to start from the top and review everything which is tedious and drop random bits of information I've kept until I find the one that was necessary for the story to continue which means I really can't choose what I keep or don't keep,

or I straight up give all the info away from the start to not have to review everything later once I'm stuck which again means I can't choose what I keep or don't keep.

There seems to be a system of highlighting the files where there still is relevant information but I don't understand how it works. Sometimes files are highlighted and there's nothing left on them and sometimes they aren't highlighted and there's still important things on them. It's very confusing.

I also suspect the political messaging of the game is really not so subtle and just "violence is bad" with no nuance but I can't tell you for sure because I'm too frustrated with the gameplay to go to the end of the story at this point. My other issue with the writing that I just can't seem to get over is that it makes zero sense that people who are fighting surveillance would post on the internet about it with their full name and photo or extremely basic aliases. Not posting about your actions on the internet is activism 101.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more.

I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]TL:DR[/h1]

If you expect the real CONSEQUENCES of YOUR actions - do not buy this game.
If you're ok with a tell-tale game with mostly textual narrative and poor amount of player choices - it's actually a good one and you really should try it. I only gave it thumb down because I'm personally not okay with the whole thing.

[h1]Now, the long review[/h1]

At first glance the game looks like a game about consequences. And it really tries to look like one. But in fact, it’s not. In the description they say "the information you supply will have consequences", but most of the game scriptwriters just lead you by the hand. It’s like playing a visual novel with dialogue options, but most of them have only one option (ridiculous, right?). Or two, both leading to the same branch but having different lines as reactions to them.
You see a chunk of info that will certainly make Symes do the wrong thing, because it's out of context, so you decide to omit it. BUT for the further story development it either won't affect a thing, or will be required for the script to go on.
You see the connection between two personages, it’s drawn at the relationships net after you add the corresponding datachunk. But you cannot fill the profile of that new guy, until he’s not a “target”, even tho you have tonns of info right before your eyes. Given there’s often no police records on the suspects, sometimes you’d really have done better with just google, no orwell system needed. So basically in Orwell you just search for the highlighted text in docs or chats and click on it.
And since there were no crucial info in all the unhighlighted text walls (and even if there were, you couldn't do anything about it if it's not highlighted as a data chunk) I've just begun to skip most of the text. The datachunks you see will lead you to the goal, and if there's a script branch, you won't miss it in most cases. But, again, it's hard to tell whether there's a branch (even for the "conflicting chunks") since there's like one real branch per day, and everything else doesn't really affect the day's outcome and seem to differ only in Symes' comments (and sometimes you can even notice mismatches in chains of his comments if you do something not in the order devs predicted ([spoiler]On the third day that Symes guy says "WOW, Harrison and Juliet were together! How interesting", while it's only UPDATE on the notion you make during the second day, Again, from 2nd day's start you get that they were together, but only at the end of the day you finally have a chance to add this to their files, therefore Symes only knows it at the end of the day, because he's out of context, which is FUKKEN STUPID AT THE FIRST PLACE[/spoiler]). 

The story is cool though. If we omit the poor gameplay and irrational investigator-symes thing, the story itself is really thrilling. I don’t think I’d last till the end of the first episode f it wasn’t for the story. 
 
But the story is not enough to recommend this piece of art as a game. Its gameplay and theme seem to be about choices, but in fact it’s just a point-and-click with prescripted everything.
Yet it’d be a great BOOK, if the player and Symes were united into single main character. Or it could be a good game with more VN-like gameplay (and again, division into invest and Symes-thing is YET WOULD BE ridiculous). But when you have a whole spy system at your control, you expect much more freedom.
Or, perhaps, that’s exactly the point - there’s no freedom in this game?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. It highlights what in that page you are supposed to save. It tells you when you have collected all of the information from that page and moves on to the next one. The entire game is just looking at these pages, or conversations, and dragging highlighted text or photos to a folder. That's it.
This game doesn't require thinking, not really. I thought the fact that you could choose what text you send over meant you could omit anything you wanted, but then it won't move on to the next series of pages. You have to send it something, and it pretty much all leads to the same outcomes.
It could have been a lot better. If it wasn't so linear, if you were left to search and find things on your own, if you could pick out which people to build a dossier on, anything like that would have made this awesome.

review_text_raw:
Okay... I don't usually write game reviews. I generally have a pretty good idea of what I'm buying beforehand on Steam, and if a game is shit it's usually because I paid for shit. But this fucking game got me.

The biggest trick is that little "Choice Matters" tag that people gave it. I love choice games. The replay value of finding every unique ending alone usually makes it worth the price. There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

review_text_raw:
Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.
[*]Music: 1 main repetitive theme loop + some other drama stings...
[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible

- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

Orwell is a "profession simulator" style interactive novel where you control a privacy invading government employee, reading peoples emails and watching security cameras.  You're forced to make decisions to progress the story, although in a bit of hamfisted design, the developers obscure a lot of the readily available information you would have just to make the game more "interesting". 

The game is a very dry computer operation simulator where you're stuck using a fake web browser to plod through the tedious game, copying text and clicking on this and that.   I'm sure there's a "watching paint dry" simulator on Steam and it would be just as engaging.  Bonus points for the sheer irony of a game about big brother asking you for your email address so they can spam you and collect data on you.  That kind of dodginess is completely reprehensible, so even if the game was actually any good, I still wouldn't recommend it to make sure the developers are getting the message.

You can never be wrong putting a clue because you get corrected or the guy confirms that the clue is correct and explains it, it just feels like you're on a tutorial mode the entire game. Also, the fact that you can't change the clues you added or erase them is a pain. You can prevent that by hovering over a clue to see what it will add, but I didn't know that because this game bugged so much that the information didn't appear until mid-game.

The story is simple and I found it okay. It has some plot twists, etc., but it is very long for its worth. There are multiple endings, and just to get one is very confusing because it feels like every possible ending is being thrown at you and you have to pick one. I already forced myself to finish one, and I don't think I will launch this game again.

Overall, if you're looking for a small investigation game or want to feel like a detective, pass on this game. It would have been a great mobile game, but is tedious on PC.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though. Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope. This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
As a game, it's way too scripted and practically visual novel -like, allowing practically no freedom of action for the player in what is presented as an interactive plot system.

Orwell does present a good criticism of government security and crime-fighting total surveillance programs that have been popping up around the world for at least the last decade. The story highlights many of the fundamental issues with such programs. It's just a pity that the story experience is ruined by the restrictive gameplay system, that forces you to do things in a silly way and backtrack to earlier data sources to use data blocks only later unlocked..

A key plot device element that got totally overlooked in the game design is that an attentive player could turn the use of the Orwell system on its head quite early on significantly affecting the story outcome to fit the canon narrative, but this is simply not possible in the game.
